messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Evan, a 28-year-old European American financial analyst, had been doing well by ordinary measures before his son’s illness, working long hours during the week and returning home each evening to a small apartment he shared with his wife. The crisis began when his toddler suddenly became gravely unwell, spiking a frightening fever and being rushed through emergency rooms and inpatient tests before doctors could stabilize him. Evan remembers the hours as a chain of fluorescent hallways, clipped voices, and the crushing sense that his child might die while he stood there unable to fix it. Since that period, certain moments have become loaded with alarm: a breaking-news alert about a pediatric illness, a stretch of cold rain outside the office windows, or a colleague’s child appearing in the break room can all make his body tighten before he has even had time to think. In those moments he reacts as if something terrible is about to happen, scanning exits in restaurants and conference rooms, choosing seats nearest the door, and lying awake at night needing to stay alert because he cannot trust that he will be ready if danger comes again.

What Evan finds most disturbing is that the fear does not stay on the surface. The same weather that once coincided with the hospital calls now seems to carry the illness back into the present for him, and the sight of children in public makes his attention snap to the possibility of loss. He has come to believe that his mind has changed in a way he cannot recognize, that he no longer knows himself, and that the man he has become is unfamiliar even to him. He often says that he should have protected others and failed, a belief that takes on particular force when he sees news about sick children or hears parents talking in the grocery store. Those reminders make him feel newly implicated, as if the world is asking him again whether he will be ready next time, and he cannot bear that question. At work, after an email about a pediatric charity event or a news clip on someone’s screen, he will find himself stepping away, checking the hall, and trying to calm the surge of dread by planning how he could get out quickly if something happened.

His memory of the illness remains strikingly vivid and detailed, but it comes to him mostly in pictures: the small body under hospital blankets, the red glow of monitor lights, his wife’s hand gripping the chair arm, the doctor’s mouth moving while he waited for the verdict. At the same time, he finds himself pushing the memory away before he can fully recall it, stopping short whenever the images start to assemble into a complete scene. He has learned that if he lets himself follow the memory all the way through, he is flooded with the same shame and sense of failure, and that makes the images come back even more sharply. The pictures then seem to confirm what he already fears about himself—that he was not enough, that he should have done more—and that conviction keeps the memory close even as he tries to shut it down.

Those memories, in turn, have made the present feel dangerous in a way he cannot shake. When he notices the first dark clouds before a storm, or hears a news segment about a child’s hospitalization, he feels the old hospital terror rush back and immediately starts scanning for ways to leave, as if every room might become another waiting room. Children present the hardest test of all: at family gatherings he stands rigidly near the door, watching the children play and feeling the same need to escape and prepare that he felt in the hospital. The more he notices these cues, the more he believes they are proof that he has changed into someone unstable and failed, which makes him want to keep the memory at bay and stay away from anything that could bring it forward again. Over weeks, that pattern has narrowed his life; he avoids staying late at the office when a storm is rolling in, turns off the television when medical stories appear, and has begun declining invitations where friends’ children will be present, leaving his wife to explain his absences.

By the time he sought help, Evan was sleeping poorly because he needed to stay alert, checking the apartment locks and mentally rehearsing how to get out of buildings before he could relax in them. He was most afraid that he would remain permanently unrecognizable to himself and that his constant sense of danger would keep him from being the father and husband he wants to be. What brought him in was the realization that he was no longer simply remembering the illness; he was organizing his days around it, and he feared that if he did not get help he would keep living as though his son’s near-death were happening all over again.
